title: QGD + C3 Sicilian | The Sensei Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: We answer c5 with our workhorse — the c3 Sicilian, in my view the best Sicilian to face for anyone under 1900.
teaches: The c3 Sicilian is a reliable anti-Sicilian below 1900

moves.spoken: He plays e6, a common reply at this level, and we grab the center with d4.
The trade on d4 is already a little inaccurate — it hands us the c3-square for the knight, giving us almost a perfect French position, though only if he follows with d5 to contest the center.
teaches: ...cxd4 cxd4 hands White a natural French-style center

moves.spoken: He develops the knight to f6 instead. Tempting as e5 looks here, there's no need to give up the d5-square — after e5 his knight just hops into d5 and entrenches on that hole.
teaches: Don\u2019t push e5 if it concedes a strong outpost on d5

moves.spoken: So we develop the knight to c3. And the pin with Bb4 that's coming is nothing to fear.

He pins with the bishop to b4. Note the moves we avoid: f3 is horribly weakening — never play it in the opening; and Bg5 is a common mistake, because he plays h6 and g5 chasing the bishop, and once it retreats the e4-pawn hangs. A counter-pin is a flimsy way to defend.
teaches: Never weaken with f3 in the opening
A counter-pin is a flimsy defense if it leaves a pawn hanging

moves.spoken: The correct move is the bishop to d3, a clean developing square eyeing the kingside.
He plays d5, and I'm already smelling a Greek gift. Crucially, we don't take on d5 — that lets him recapture with the knight and hand us an isolated queen pawn under blockade.
teaches: Avoid trades that saddle you with a blockaded isolated pawn

moves.spoken: The move is to push e5, gaining space and shutting the door — this should be clear to everyone.
He jumps the knight into e4. Now the adventurous, instructive choice: castle, offering the c3-knight and prioritizing development — the very same idea as a main-line Italian.
teaches: Sacrifice a pawn for a development lead when the attack is real

moves.spoken: We castle. I keep the dark-squared bishop rather than trading it, because our d4-pawn sits on a dark square and I want to defend it later with Be3.
teaches: Keep the bishop that guards your weak-colored squares

moves.spoken: He grabs on c3, and if you know the main-line Italian, this whole structure should feel familiar.
Rb1 — and here's the trap: if he tries the knight fork on d4, remember from last game that a forking knight can simply return to c6 and block the fork.
teaches: A forked knight can often retreat to block the fork

moves.spoken: He does grab on d4. We just take the knight first, and now a check picks up the piece cleanly.
teaches: Remove the defender first, then collect the fork

moves.spoken: Now we switch fronts: the rook lifts to b3, ready to swing to the kingside. Look how bare his king is — once the bishop clears d3, this rook comes over for the mating attack.
teaches: A rook lift can transfer an attack to the other wing
plans: Swing it to the kingside for the attack

moves.spoken: The Greek gift — bishop takes h7. It's not as clear-cut as it looks, but it's winning, and it's worth seeing.
I start with the queen check on h4 — a flexible entry. The point: Qh4 then Rh3 does NOT force immediate mate, because f6 opens an escape for the king. Always check the escape before you commit.
teaches: Qh4+ first keeps the attack flexible
Verify the king has no escape before sacrificing further

moves.spoken: And the constructive idea — look at the semi-open files too, not just the open ones. That g7-pawn is pitiful cover, so the rook to g3 sets up Qf6, Bh6, and a sac on g7.
teaches: Attack down semi-open files where the pawn cover is thin
